items.question: How do you see the limitations of human-designed agent workflows compared with letting models learn a process through rewards?
items.object: Human-designed agent workflows versus models that learn through rewards
items.answer: The way I see it, in, let's say 2023, 2024, the way most people were trying to build agents is a human designs a system and that system kind of breaks the problem down into multiple steps. It assigns each of those steps to an LLM. Maybe there's some rules built in, but often times the real world is messy and that workflow that you built might be an oversimplification of the actual process a real expert at this task would follow. And when models are able to learn how to do the process by being rewarded for succeeding at the process, they're able to figure out in many cases something that's better than you could easily sit down and design yourself.

items.question: How has the rise of general-purpose AI models changed your thinking about whether businesses should train their own models?
items.object: Building on foundation models versus training business-specific models
items.answer:
I think in the pre-ChatGPT era, a lot of companies' mental models were that every company is going to need to be training models. Before we had GPT-3 and later models that did this more effectively, the thinking was the way to create actual value with AI is to train models that are fit for purpose for the thing that your business needs to do. So there's a whole category of infrastructure that was built under the assumption that every business out there is going to be training its own models in the future. And so what tool will they need?

I think what turned out to be true is that general-purpose models, GPT-3, GPT-4, other large language models, are quite good at most tasks that you can specify for any given domain. You might be able to build a better model than GPT-4, but it's going to be pretty hard and pretty expensive. If there's an off-the-shelf model that can just do those things well for you, it's so much faster, cheaper, more efficient for every business to build on top of that commercially provided model instead of building up all the infrastructure expertise, data, and domain-specific knowledge that you need in order to build the model yourself.

I think that didn't fully invalidate it, but it made the business model that a lot of that crop of ML infrastructure startups was thinking about a lot less feasible. Now my operating assumption, when I advise companies on how to think about ML, is I generally tell them: don't even think about training your own models until you've exhausted what you can do with the models that OpenAI or any other foundation model provider will sell you.

items.question: What do you think is needed to make AI agents reliable enough for people to delegate multistep work to them?
items.object: Reliable AI agents for multistep workflows
items.answer:
Before I came back to OpenAI, I had spent a little bit of time tinkering, building agents on top of LLM APIs. The problem that we ran into, which I think is the problem pretty much everyone runs into when they try to build their own agents using workflows on top of LLM API calls, is that it's very tempting to think, "Oh, LLMs are good at making point predictions, making decisions. So we build a workflow around this LLM. Then we can automate a process and take a bunch of decisions and turn it into something that just happens on its own."

But what a lot of us found trying to do this is that the temptation is there because you can create a demo of this very quickly that looks great. But when you try to actually deploy this and get people to stop doing this work themselves and instead delegate it to an agent, you start to run into all kinds of edge cases and failure modes, and getting things to work reliably is really hard.

The root cause of the problem is that most LLMs historically have not been trained to do agentic work. At any given step of the process, maybe they're relatively accurate because they're pretty smart general-purpose AI systems. But as you run a process that requires many steps, the small errors at one step compound as you take multiple steps. Even if you're 90% accurate on one step, if you have to take 10 steps, then your accuracy will fall off. That's the core challenge of building agents on top of traditional LLMs.

The missing ingredient has been that we need to directly train these agents end to end to do these workflow-like tasks. By doing that, you can train the agents so that they see failures during their training and learn to recover from those failures. Even if each step is only 90% or 95% accurate, now the model has seen what it looks like to fail at that step and is able to reroute itself. It's able to think, "Oh, this doesn't look right. Let me go back and try that again."

items.question: Why do you see end-to-end reinforcement learning as key to making web research agents recover from mistakes?
items.object: End-to-end reinforcement learning for web research agents
items.answer:
A good example would be if you're trying to build an agent that does research for you. If you do a single web search and maybe you get the search term wrong—the user doesn't know exactly what to search for—so you try terms that seem relevant and start to pull back a bunch of docs that don't have information that really gets to the heart of the problem. A naive agent might just get confused by that and think, "Okay, I searched for the term that I thought that they meant, and all these docs are irrelevant, so maybe what the user asked for doesn't make sense, or maybe I need to go down this other rabbit hole."

Whereas an agent that's trained to do web research and has been trained using reinforcement learning to be good at this multi-step process will, in its training, have seen many instances where it searched for the wrong term. The training has incentivized it to learn to recover from those instances and instead go back and think, "I searched for this term, but I got results that weren't relevant. Maybe that means I had the wrong search term. So let me try again and pick a different one."

The key is really reasoning models that are trained end to end to solve the kinds of tasks that users need them to solve, using reinforcement learning so that they're able to see these multi-step processes, see the kinds of failures that happen in training, and learn to recover from them.

items.question: How do you see improvements in models like O3 changing the difficulty of building custom agents?
items.object: O3 and the prospects for building custom agents
items.answer: Well, I do think as the models get better, building these types of workflows will be a lot easier. Already, I think O3 is quite good compared to older models at being able to understand the level of complexity of instructions that you often have to have to automate a process or build a complicated workflow. It's better at adhering to those instructions and using tools over multi-step trajectories than anything else that came before it. I still think there's a ways to go before that is a generally useful agent. But as the models get better, building custom agents is going to get dramatically easier.

items.question: How do you think about the relative strengths of small and large models for custom agentic applications?
items.object: Small versus large models for custom agentic applications
items.answer: I don't think we've really exhausted our limit of how good we can make small models. But I think the advantages that large models have are that they tend to be better at generalization. Most of the time, if you're building something custom on top of models, that thing might not be something that the developers of the model anticipated. So larger models will tend to work a little bit better.

items.question: Why do you see a model's ability to choose its reasoning effort as important for agentic workflows?
items.object: Adaptive reasoning effort in agentic workflows
items.answer: I think the other feature of models for agentic use cases that's really valuable is reasoning. A lot of agentic tasks have this quality where there's a range in difficulty levels of solving the task, and doing the right thing at each step is very important to make sure that the overall task succeeds. Letting the model choose how much reasoning effort it wants to apply to figure out the current step of the workflow feels like a pretty important component of what's going to make these systems work well.

items.question: What do you find surprising about using Deep Research for coding?
items.object: Deep Research for coding
items.answer: I think when people think about Deep Research, they think about using it for market research and scientific literature review and other tasks where the model has to go out and think and read a lot of documents to come back with a synthesized answer. But some of the other things that people are using it for, which were initially surprising to us, are coding. Even though we didn't really design the model for this use case, there's a lot of code publicly available on the internet, and because of the capabilities in the base model, it's able to understand it very well. It's able to search and find code on GitHub, understand how different pieces of the codebase work, and come back to you with descriptions of the code or plans for how to implement a feature.

items.question: Why do you consider finding rare facts on the internet an underrated use of Deep Research?
items.object: Deep Research for finding rare facts
items.answer: I think the other underrated use of Deep Research is finding very rare facts on the internet. Most people use Deep Research to go broad and then synthesize: go read about this topic and come back with a summary covering these points, where the model has to touch a bunch of different topics. But the model is also quite good at finding information that's buried in the corner of the internet somewhere. If you want to recall details of some television episode that you saw a long time ago, maybe something specific enough that it wouldn't just be on the Wikipedia page, often the model will be able to find that one fan page or something from 10 years ago and point to that information too.

items.question: What would you love ChatGPT to become in terms of how it understands and responds to your questions?
items.object: ChatGPT as a personal assistant that judges how much research a question needs
items.answer: I think the thing that I would love ChatGPT to become is a place where you can just go and it's like talking to your friend and your coworker and your personal assistant and your coach all in one. You could ask a question like you would to a person. Just like a great coworker would, it knows when to come back to you with a really quick answer off the top of its head versus, from the context and from knowing you, when it should actually go and do a bunch of research and come back to you with something more thorough.

items.question: How would you like ChatGPT to evolve as a collaborator during research?
items.object: ChatGPT as a natural collaborator during research
items.answer:
It's like, yeah, here's the answer off the top of my head, but I'll go dig into this a little bit more. Or it could come back and, like, in Deep Research, there's this phase in the beginning where it'll ask you a few follow-up questions. But I think eventually it should be able to just come back to you in the middle of its research and say, "Hey, here's what I'm finding so far. I'm going to keep going, but is there any feedback? Do you have any feedback on this? Is this what you're imagining? Or now that you've seen this, are there any other avenues that you want me to explore?"

So I think evolving ChatGPT into an entity that feels a lot more natural to co-work with is one of the main things that I hope we're able to achieve.

items.question: Why do you think the initial back and forth with Deep Research leads to better results?
items.object: Deep Research’s initial follow-up questions
items.answer:
What we found is that since Deep Research is designed to go deep and collect a lot of information and come back to you with a very detailed report, it is really excellent at covering all the finer points or nuances of the initial framing of the question that you wrote. The quality of the results that you get is sensitive to—you get better results if you put time up front into thinking about what you really want to see at the end. The model is very good at adhering to those things and incorporating the different parts of the question that you asked into its search.

The model will also come back with reasonable answers if you just fire off a quick question to it. But the upfront back and forth is meant to help flesh out a more detailed thing to run by the model because we think it produces more compelling results.

items.question: How do you see conversational models helping you frame a question for Deep Research when you don't know much about the topic?
items.object: Using conversational models to frame questions for Deep Research
items.answer: I know from experience you can suggest that you're not sure how to frame the question and that you might want some—you can prompt it to ask you questions, and that works just fine as well. One thing that we've seen a lot of people do is use O1 or now O3 or O4 Mini to help craft the question. If there's a topic where you don't even really know enough to frame a good question, a lot of times folks will have a conversation with a smaller model and use that to flesh out all the details of the question that they want to research. Then they'll put that into Deep Research and have it spend 10 or 20 minutes coming up with a much more research response.

items.question: How do you define an agentic AI system?
items.object: Agentic systems
items.answer: I think of an agentic system as any AI system that is able to go work on tasks for you that take longer than a few seconds and that has to interact with the real world in order to solve your problem. Operator, Deep Research, and Codex CLI are all good examples of agentic systems.

items.question: How do you think about Operator’s usefulness at its current stage of development?

items.answer:
The technology to make Operator work really well is an incredibly difficult thing to build. Operator is not intended to be the thing that every single person in the world uses every day on day one. It was meant to be an early launch of this technology so that people could get value from it and could also get a feel for where this is going.

Despite that, there are a bunch of people who use this a lot—power users. I think of it a lot like the early GPT-3 API, if you remember that. I don't think OpenAI would have framed it this way at the time, but in a lot of ways it was a technology preview: something where most people tried it and were like, "Oh, this is really amazing. It's amazing that humanity has created this thing," but they didn't immediately find it useful. Even on day one with GPT-3, there were a bunch of people who were really drawn to the technology. I think Operator is more at that stage of model development, where there are power users who love it, but it's not for everyone yet.

items.question: Why do you see OpenAI's local code execution agent Codex as a powerful demonstration of where AI coding systems are going?
items.object: OpenAI's local code execution agent Codex
items.answer: Codex is our local code execution agent. It's a package that's fully open source that you can install on your laptop. Then you can talk to it and ask it questions about your code, or ask it to implement things in your codebase. This agent is able to use your computer to navigate the file system, find the relevant files, understand how they work, write code on its own, apply those patches to your files, run tests, try things out, and come back to you when it has an answer to your question, or it's written some unit tests or some code or whatever you really want it to do. I think it's a really powerful demonstration of where AI systems for coding are going, and people are loving it so far. People at OpenAI use it a ton. There's more than 20,000 stars on GitHub, which is amazing to me. Around 100 people have contributed to it.

items.question: How do you distinguish the work you find agentic coding tools useful for from the work best served by AI-powered IDE functionality?
items.object: Agentic coding tools versus AI-powered IDE functionality
items.answer:
Most software engineers here use Codex CLI and potentially some AI-powered functionality in their IDE. They're used for slightly different things. The IDE functionality is great because when you're writing code, you're most of the time inside the IDE anyway. Those tools are amazing for having very quick access to the AI system in your flow state. If you're in the middle of writing some code, you can get a suggestion or delegate something to a model, and then just keep going with what you're doing.

These agentic tools are better for, or at least I find myself and a lot of folks find themselves using them more for, de novo type work, where maybe you're just at the start of the project, or you're working in a codebase for the first time, or you have an idea for a feature that you want to build that's not literally the thing that you're working on at the moment, but something you might want to delegate to someone else. That's when this agentic paradigm becomes really powerful.

items.question: How do you envision coding agents evolving beyond the way Codex CLI works today?
items.object: The progression from Codex CLI to autonomous coding agents
items.answer:
Today, the way the Codex CLI works is you give it a task to do and it does it on your laptop. One of the really cool things is that it's able to do it in a network-sandboxed way, meaning it can work for you in a way that is safe because it's not able to hit the network, so it's not able to accidentally run some unsafe command or something like that. But it's still running on your laptop, so you still need to have your laptop open and watch it as it goes.

Over time, where this is going is that interacting with these coding agents should feel more and more like delegating to someone, where they're able to take larger and larger chunks of work and execute them more and more autonomously. If you have 10 things on your to-do list in the morning, maybe you go work on one and come back at the end of the day and the other nine have been finished for you. That's the paradigm of agentic coding, and we're not there yet, but that's where we're trying to get to.

items.question: How do you think about delegating coding tasks to the Codex CLI given its lack of context about your codebase?
items.object: Codex CLI as a contextless coding agent
items.answer:
I think the Codex CLI, you can almost think of it as a contextless tool. My mental model for giving a task to the Codex CLI is that it's like giving a task to a superhuman intern who has never seen your codebase before. That's only a little oxymoronic: an intern because you can't really trust it yet with really complicated stuff where you need a lot of state or experience working on this particular type of project, where there's a lot of different pieces that need to be broken down. I think you want to delegate intern-sized chunks of work to it. Superhuman because it's able to read code, write code, understand code, understand coding patterns much faster than any human can.

It is seeing your codebase for the first time because it is contextless. When you start a new task in the Codex CLI, the model has to explore the codebase on its own before it can start working on the task. The way it does it is pretty amazing. It's not using bespoke context management tools or ideas. It's just using the same command-line tools that people have been using for decades.

items.question: How do you think about the context models need to work effectively in a codebase with the Codex CLI?
items.object: Context and codebase understanding in Codex CLI models
items.answer:
It turns out, which I think is really surprising, that the model is able to build an understanding of how to navigate the codebase, find the information it needs, where to write code, and what the patterns in the codebase are extremely quickly just by exploring the file system.

Coming back to the magic of training models using reinforcement learning to achieve an outcome: this is the type of magic that emerges when you do that type of training. Models are able to learn how to use tools really effectively to achieve their goals. My impression is that these models are much more efficient than humans at how much code they need to read before they're able to actually build something. That's how I think about context for these models.

That being said, I do think we could improve on this by giving the models more context or richer customization. Right now there's a way to customize the behavior of the models by placing a file in the repository, but you can imagine all kinds of other types of customization too, like giving APIs or MCPs to the model. You can imagine giving the model memory so it can remember things between rollouts. These are lots of ideas that we're exploring for how to make the models even better at understanding the specifics of your codebase and get smarter as they interact with it more.

items.question: How do you think AI coding systems will change the work of developing software?
items.object: AI-driven changes to software development
items.answer:
I think we're in the early phases of a dramatic shift in the way software is built. I don't think writing code is ever going to go away, but the process of manually writing code, where you have to write down every single line of code yourself, manually test it, think through the architecture, and do each of these pieces by hand, is going to become rarer and rarer. I think the vast majority of code is going to be written by AI systems much sooner than people think.

The job of developing software is going to become a lot more like thinking about the functionality you want the system to have, thinking about the trade-offs and edge cases, guiding the AI system, providing feedback to it, and finding ways to validate its work. I think the nature of the work is going to change, and people who write code are going to become much more productive.

items.question: How do you see AI changing the boundaries between engineering, design, and product roles in software development?
items.object: AI-driven changes in the boundaries between engineering, design, and product roles
items.answer:
I think it is part of a shift that's already happening. As programming has moved up in abstraction over time, the ability of one person to bridge the entire span of programming has gotten bigger. We're already seeing the proliferation, especially in the startup world, of design engineers—folks who are great designers and can also build the things they design—or technical product managers, or full-stack engineers who can write front-end and backend code.

I think this accelerates that. Your engineering skill set is still really valuable, but less of your mental energy will be devoted to learning the nuances or ins and outs of a particular framework or language, and more of your mental energy will be devoted to thinking about how things work, what they do, why we do things a certain way, and how we know it's working well. That gives people space to think about a bigger chunk of the problem than they did before.

Maybe this is a controversial opinion, but I still think it's important for people to learn programming, even if it's a smaller percentage of what they're going to spend their time doing if they want to build software.

In grad school for machine learning, there are some rites-of-passage type activities, like building a computer from scratch or building a backpropagation library from scratch, from first principles. Is this the single thing you can do that will maximize your ability to perform your machine learning research or job the best next week? No. 99% of the time when you're doing machine learning, you don't need to understand the way backpropagation works at a very fundamental level. However, when things go wrong, being able to spelunk all the way down the stack and think through, "Okay, well, this isn't working. Why isn't it working?"—having a fundamental understanding of pieces lower in the stack is really important to being able to do that efficiently.

A lot of people who have gone through that exercise will tell you, "Every once in a while, I do have to think about this, and I realize this is where the bug came from; it's something about the way backpropagation is working." I think the same will be true for code for a long time. If you aspire to be really good at this, there will be a lot of cases where being able to look at the code that the model wrote, even though you'll do it less and less, is still very much worth your time. The people who are able to do that well will be better at this more vibe-coding style of coding than the people who can't.

items.question: How do you see tool access fitting into the formula for useful AI agents?
items.object: Tool access as part of building useful AI agents
items.answer:
I think exposing tools to a model—if you think about the formula for useful agents, in my mind it's like you have to have a really smart, general-purpose reasoning model, and then expose it to the tools it needs to do the thing it needs to do. Hopefully, you should provide a relatively small amount of high-quality, task-specific training to teach the model how to do the thing that you want it to do.

Being able to expose the tools to the model in a way that it's able to use them both for training and for doing the task in the real world is a really critical piece of how the ecosystem fits together. Everyone is thinking about this now for good reason.

items.question: What do you see as an underdeveloped part of how AI agents are allowed to use tools?
items.object: Specifying and enforcing trust in AI agents’ use of tools
items.answer:
One thing that feels not fully developed yet is the ability to specify a level of trust for the agent using certain tools. The future that everyone is picturing is you'll ask ChatGPT to book a vacation, it'll know you really well, do a bunch of research, come back, charge your credit card, and send you the itinerary, hopefully asking you a bunch of questions along the way if it needs to. But doing something like using your credit card is a very high-trust act. Exposing your credit card to an agent that you don't trust, or exposing it without specifying how and when you wanted it to use the card, is a very scary idea and potentially super risky.

One thing I feel like the field doesn't have a great handle on yet is how to build in ways of specifying and enforcing certain levels of trust between the human, the agent, the tool, and the task, so that you can just ask the agent to do something and it knows when it needs to come ask you for permission to use certain tools based on your interactions with it so far.

items.question: How do you think permission guidelines should work for AI agents performing high-risk actions such as using your credit card?
items.object: Permission guidelines and trust in AI agents performing high-risk actions
items.answer:
I think at a fundamental level what it comes down to is having a set of guidelines that you can provide to the agent about when it needs to come get your permission to use certain tools. The most strict version would be providing the guidelines and also having some mechanism to enforce them, or some level of trust that the guidelines will be followed.

The simplest example would be a guideline that says, "You have access to a credit card tool, but every time you call the credit card tool, you need to come ask me to approve." Then you don't need to have a lot of trust in the model to use that tool because you always have the opportunity to review what it did. Now there's still problems of deception, because the model might try to misrepresent what it did or what its goals of using the tool are. But at least you have the opportunity to say no.

You still have to have a high degree of trust in the agent, even if you specify some set of parameters. I think it's an interesting question whether the current crop of models, model architecture, the way we train models, or the state of alignment warrants that trust, and it depends on the task and the model. Building that trust to do high-risk actions will need to be something model developers and product developers think carefully about. Users will need to build that trust iteratively through interacting with the model. I think there's still a lot of thought we need to do as an industry to figure out how to make that work.

items.question: How do you think about who should bear the risk when an AI agent makes a payment on your behalf?
items.object: Trust and residual risk in payments made by AI agents
items.answer: There are technical and political solutions to the problem. Actually, Visa is going to take the role of providing some degree of trust by allowing me to beat them up when the agent does stupid things. That could be interesting and useful. I don't think they will. But there will be residual risk there, and I do think there's an interesting question of to what degree these different parties should bear that residual risk. Is it a risk that I take on as a user? Is it something where the model provider is saying that it's okay? Maybe the payment provider. It'll certainly be interesting to see how it plays out.
quotes: That's both pointing out the timeliness of this conversation and the fact that there are technical and political solutions to the problem.
